cards.editorialAnalysis: Easy fails plausible alternatives (guide lines 5,17): a vehicle on the rink cannot sharpen worn skate blades; drawing permanent face-off markings and repairing boards are not credible intermission resurfacer jobs. Nominal labels read grammatically and notes are substantive. The key and six facts are supported, but broad maintenance category alone does not make every option plausible.

fields.claimAnalysis: IIHF Ice Resurfacer directly supports cleaning/smoothing. Distractors sharpening skates and repairing boards are mechanically implausible jobs for a vehicle driving on ice; easy requires all four credible.
Hockey Canada physical PDF page 8 explicitly recommends regular sharpening for grip and glide. The skate-blade note accurately describes sharpening; no attribution to the vehicle.
IIHF Face-Off Circles and Spots explicitly locates face-offs for resumption of play. The Russian note is a short accurate standalone description.
IIHF Ice Resurfacer calls Zamboni a colloquial term and brand name, matching the note without implying a unique machine manufacturer.
IIHF Boards or Wall describes enclosing boards and protective glass above them, directly supporting both clauses.
IIHF supports cleaning/smoothing and the colloquial brand name. Two sentences state the answer and useful naming clarification; no unsupported extra fact.

cards.editorialAnalysis: Easy fails the premise exclusion rule: asking the program before the free program while offering that same free program yields an impossible self-predecessor. Free/rhythm dances are recognizably pair dance formats against singles. Grammar and source facts pass; source is Canadian Olympic Committee, not FIS.

fields.claimAnalysis: COC states top 24 singles from short programs advance to free skates. The key is supported, but free program cannot be its own preceding stage; easy all-four plausibility fails.
COC free dance paragraph describes couples and dance lifts, spins and sequences. Note accurately identifies pair dance elements.
COC singles short-program paragraph explicitly lists jumping passes, spins and a step sequence.
COC rhythm dance paragraph explicitly assigns season theme and/or rhythms. Note preserves alternatives rather than overclaiming both always required.
COC singles free-skate paragraph explicitly admits the top 24 from the short program. Useful note overlaps the main fact legitimately.
The qualification order in the complete COC original supports short then free, and participants determined by short-program results. Two clear sentences.

cards.editorialAnalysis: Easy all-four plausible rule fails: gloves, elbow pads and shin pads explicitly name other body locations and are obviously not headwear. The shared protection category and four grammatically consistent nominal answers do not remove this body-part elimination cue. All six factual claims have direct Hockey Canada support.

fields.claimAnalysis: Physical PDF page 13 helmet fit above eyebrows/on chin establishes headwear. Alternatives explicitly protect hands/elbows/shins, making the answer immediate from ordinary word meanings rather than four plausible choices.
Physical PDF page 13 requires a snug chinstrap to prevent wobbling; note preserves meaning.
Physical PDF page 14 explicitly says gloves protect hands, wrists, fingers and help grip the stick.
Physical PDF page 10 explicitly states elbows and forearms; note is exact and standalone.
Physical PDF page 5 says shin pads protect from knee to top of skate, supporting both shin and knee.
Physical pages 13,14,10,5 collectively support the helmet/chinstrap and other body parts. Two grammatical sentences; useful repetition is permitted.

cards.editorialAnalysis: Easy fails credible same-category choices: a stick is held rather than worn and cannot be facewear; catcher/blocker are hand equipment. The verb надевает itself excludes the stick. Russian nominal labels are otherwise consistent. IIHF supports all notes and the answer.

fields.claimAnalysis: IIHF Face Mask supports goalkeeper face protection, but stick is not something worn and hand gloves cannot credibly protect the face while worn. Premise/category cues violate easy plausibility.
IIHF Catching Glove says non-stick hand; Russian wording preserves this precisely.
IIHF Face Mask explicitly covers goalkeepers and women players. Note claims face protection also used by female field players, without claiming identical masks.
IIHF Blocker explicitly says stick-holding hand and blocking shots on that side; note accurate.
IIHF Stick defines the goalkeeper stick as having wider blade and shaft. Note limits shaft wording to lower part, consistent with goalie paddle terminology; no numerical specification added.
IIHF Face Mask, Blocker and Catching Glove collectively support mask/face and gloves/hands. Two readable sentences.

cards.editorialAnalysis: Easy fails all-four plausible: gloves, boots and ski bindings cannot cover the eyes while retaining vision. Body-location mismatch makes three choices obviously impossible. FIS source title/institution is appropriate; terminology and four nominal labels read clearly. Notes and explanation have direct full-PDF support.

fields.claimAnalysis: FIS physical PDF page 35 section 3.7 defines eye/weather/ray protection and good visibility. Boots, gloves and bindings are impossible eye coverings in this premise, violating easy plausibility.
Physical PDF page 35 section 3.8 explicitly describes gloves as protective covering against weather and external forces.
Physical PDF page 25 section 3.2.1 defines ski boots as robust footwear protecting from jolts, bumps, ski edges and external influences.
Physical PDF page 35 section 3.7 explicitly prohibits reshaping goggles for aerodynamic advantages.
Physical PDF page 24 section 3.1.4.1 defines binding release when loads reach preset values. Boot fixation follows binding/boot attachment; the note correctly combines retention and release.
Physical PDF page 35 section 3.7 supports eye protection, all-weather visibility and optically correct lenses. Two sentences satisfy explanation limits.
